HINGLISH, must fix: bookish pronouns. l03 uses 'यह' twice and l08 uses 'वह'. Nobody in Mumbai or UP says 'yah/vah' in speech; they say 'ये/वो'. Plan section 2 says the written text is exactly what the voice reads and what the subtitle shows, so the voice may say 'vah' in the single most important line of the scene.

LENGTH: the per-line targets are optimistic, so the real cut will run about 33 to 35 s, not 30.5. The caller is directed as 'completely unhurried' yet has the densest lines: l07 at 12 characters per second and l08 at 13.1, against 9 to 10 for everyone else. l08 also carries an ellipsis pause and a whispered second half. b7 packs ignition, wiper sweep, headlights, a hold on her face and a cut to black into 3.3 s. This is my estimate from line density, not a measured take.

PERFORMABILITY, key line at risk: the second half of l08 is the ending question itself, and it is whispered, band-limited by the phone filter, and sits over a heavy rain bed plus drone. Whispered Hindi through a narrow-band filter is the likeliest line in the scene to come out unintelligible.

PIPELINE COVERAGE and Hinglish density: only 4 Latin-script words in 3 of 10 lines (Bag, Wrong number, driver). Tara is described as 'Mumbai Hindi with easy English' but has one English phrase. Section 7.1 names timing and pronunciation on mixed Devanagari + Latin lines as the highest-risk unknown, and this proof scene barely exercises it. It also reads closer to plain Hindi than to how a 31-year-old Mumbai con artist talks.
CRAFT: l03 ('what is this?') is generic filler. The insert shot of cut newspaper already says it, and it is the weakest line in an otherwise tight script.

HOOK: the first 4.7 s are celebration and set-up (l01, l02). The actual shock, the empty bag and the phone, lands at roughly 6 to 8 s. The opening works on irony and Imran's planted 'पहले गिन लो', which is good, but it is not the strongest possible first 5 seconds for a scroll format.

CLIFFHANGER, minor: the stated ending_question ('who is Imran driving for tonight?') is spoken aloud by the caller and then largely answered by the lock, the callback line and the tail-car headlights. What is genuinely open is whether Imran is delivering her or protecting her. The triple button risks over-confirming betrayal and losing that ambiguity, and the ending_question field does not name the real open question.

CONTINUITY: Tara is 'still out of breath from running' but the taxi is parked with engine off and wipers still, and the caller says she became Nisha 'आज शाम' while the scene is at about 2 am. The gap between the evening con and a just-now bag grab is unexplained. Small, but an attentive viewer will feel it.

TAGS: l04 '[urgent]' contradicts Imran's voice note ('flat and tired, never raises his voice'). l09 stacks two tags on a one-word line, which is where tagged speech models are least stable. '[cold]' and '[deadpan]' are less common directions and are unverified on the chosen model; I did not test them.

STILLS-ONLY STAGING (section 9: no image-to-video): b6 and b7 describe about seven motion events in 6.7 s (eyes travel, hand moves, locks drop, hand stops, key turns, wiper sweeps, headlights switch on). Several can only exist as sound. b4 holds one set-up for 8.5 s, above the 8 s ceiling in section 7.3, while b2, b3 and b6 imply shots of about 1.2 to 1.7 s.

MINOR: (a) the 'language' field starts with 'hi-Latn-mixed', which literally means Hindi in Latin script, the opposite of the convention used; wrong if any tool parses it or passes it as language_code. (b) Central locking that drops all four doors in an old-engine kaali-peeli is a small authenticity stretch; low priority, the sound moment is worth keeping.
